paragraphs.text: Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – Through this application, the Petitioner seeks post-arrest bail in case FIR No.2031/2025 dated 19.06.2025 registered at Police Station Islampura, Lahore, for an offence under section 295-A of the Pakistan Penal Code 1860 (PPC).

As per the FIR, the prosecution’s case is that the Petitioner worked at the Evacuee Trust Property Board and is presently suspended from service. On 19.06.2025 at about 11:20 a.m., he came to the office and began abusing the Secretary and the Deputy Secretary and threatened to kill them. The security staff ousted him from the Secretariat, but he continued using abusive language. It is further alleged that he stated that, according to the Holy Qur’an, Hazrat Isa (A.S.) would return to the world and that, by the command of Allah Almighty, he himself was the promised Hazrat Isa. According to the FIR, many persons present there heard this assertion, which allegedly outraged the religious feelings of Muslims and Christians alike.

Ch. Muhammad Shahbaz, Advocate, contends that the Petitioner is suffering from mental illness and is undergoing medical treatment. He submits that at the time of the alleged occurrence, the Petitioner was either under the influence of prescribed medication or experiencing a bout of mental illness, and therefore lacked the requisite mens rea. Thus, his case falls within the ambit of section 84 PPC. Counsel has placed on record copies of various medical prescriptions in support of this plea.

Rana Tasawar Ali Khan, Additional Prosecutor General (APG), contends that the question whether the Petitioner is of unsound mind cannot be determined on the basis of prescriptions produced before this Court. Since the Petitioner seeks the protection of section 84 PPC, the procedure prescribed in Chapter XXXIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (the “Cr.P.C.” or the “Code of 1898”) must first be followed. According to the APG, if the Petitioner’s plea is accepted, his release would then be governed by section 466 read with section 475 Cr.P.C. Therefore, the present bail application is not maintainable.

On merits, the APG contends that the Petitioner is nominated in the FIR. PWs have made statements to the Investigating Officer, recorded under section 161 Cr.P.C., supporting the prosecution’s case, which, according to him, are corroborated by video footage of the incident. During the investigation, the police found that the Petitioner had committed the alleged offence. Hence, he is not entitled to bail.
The Complainant’s counsel, Mr. Adeel Asghar Hashmi, Advocate, has adopted the APG’s arguments.
Arguments heard. Record perused.

The insanity defence, sometimes described as the defence of legal insanity, constitutes an exception to criminal liability recognized by section 84 PPC. Under that provision, an act does not amount to an offence if it is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that what he is doing is either wrong or contrary to law. Chapter XXXIV of the Code of 1898 (sections 464 to 475) prescribes the procedure to be followed in cases involving an accused of unsound mind.

It is, however, necessary to distinguish between two related but distinct legal concepts. Section 84 PPC concerns legal insanity at the time of the commission of the alleged act and constitutes a substantive defence affecting criminal responsibility. Sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C., on the other hand, relate to the present mental condition of the accused and his capacity to understand the proceedings and make his defence. The former addresses culpability at the time of the occurrence; the latter concerns competency to stand trial.

To address the APG’s objection regarding the maintainability of this bail application, it is necessary to appreciate the statutory scheme of Chapter XXXIV of the Code of 1898. Section 464 Cr.P.C. mandates that when a Magistrate holding an inquiry or trial has reason to believe that the accused is of unsound mind and consequently incapable of making his defence, he should inquire into that fact and have the accused examined by the Civil Surgeon or such other medical officer as the Provincial Government directs. If satisfied, he should record a finding to that effect and postpone further proceedings in the case. Section 465 makes corresponding provision for trials before a Court of Session or a High Court. Upon such a finding, the question of custody or release falls to be considered under the ensuing provisions.

Section 466(1) Cr.P.C. provides that whenever an accused person is found to be of unsound mind and incapable of making his defence, the Magistrate or court, as the case may be, whether the case is one in which bail may be taken or not, may release him on sufficient security being given that he shall be properly taken care of and shall be prevented from doing injury to himself or to any other person, and for his appearance when required before the Magistrate or court or such officer as the Magistrate or court appoints in this behalf. Section 466(2) stipulates that if the case is one in which, in the opinion of the Magistrate or court, bail should not be taken, or if sufficient security is not given, the Magistrate or court, as the case may be, shall order the accused to be detained in safe custody in such place and manner as he or it may think fit, and shall report the action taken to the Provincial Government. Section 475(1) further provides that whenever any relative or friend of any person detained under section 466 desires that he may be delivered to his care and custody, he may apply to the Provincial Government, which may grant his request on his giving security to its satisfaction for the due performance of the obligations stipulated in that provision.

In this context, Safia Bano and another v. Home Department, Government of Punjab, and others (PLD 2021 SC 488) is relevant. In that case, the Supreme Court explained that the expressions “reason to believe” and “appears to the court” occurring in sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C. require the court to form a tentative opinion as to whether an inquiry into the accused’s capability to face trial is necessary. Such an opinion must rest on an objective assessment of the material placed before the court or available in the police and case files. It may also consider the accused’s conduct and demeanour and exercise this power on its own motion, even if the parties do not raise such a plea. Once a tentative opinion of possible incapacity is formed, the court is obliged to hold an inquiry, for which the accused must be examined by a Medical Board comprising qualified mental health experts. The Board’s report must not be confined to a mere diagnosis of mental illness or its absence; rather, it should provide a detailed and structured assessment of the accused’s mental functions, including consciousness, intellect, thinking, mood, emotions, perception, cognition, judgment, and insight. The head of the Medical Board should then be examined as a court witness, with full opportunity to the prosecution and the defence to cross-examine, and the parties may also adduce further evidence, including expert testimony. Upon consideration of the medical and other evidence on record, the court shall record a finding on the accused’s capability to face trial within the meaning of sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C.

Mere assertion of mental illness or invocation of section 84 PPC does not, ipso facto, amount to a judicial determination of incapacity within the meaning of sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C. However, once such a determination is made, he becomes incompetent to act on his own in the proceedings by reason of his legal incapacity. In that event, he can neither instruct a counsel nor apply to the court himself for release by way of a bail application or otherwise. Sections 466 and 475 Cr.P.C. would then govern the matter.

The APG’s aforementioned objection is premised on the assumption that once mental illness is pleaded, the procedure under Chapter XXXIV of the Code of 1898 must first be invoked. This assumption is misconceived. Until a competent court records a finding in accordance with sections 464 or 465 Cr.P.C. that the accused is of unsound mind and suffers from such incapacity, he remains legally competent to invoke the court’s jurisdiction under section 497 Cr.P.C. In the present case, no such finding has been recorded. The prescriptions relied upon by the Petitioner do not, by themselves, satisfy the procedural requirements of sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C. Therefore, this application is competent, and the APG’s objection is overruled. Nevertheless, it shall remain open to the trial court to consider the applicability of sections 464 and 465 Cr.P.C., if warranted.

The Petitioner is booked under section 295-A PPC, which was inserted into the Penal Code by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1927 (XXV of 1927). Currently, it reads as under: 295-A. Deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings of any class by insulting its religion or religious beliefs.– Whoever, with deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings, or any class of the citizens of Pakistan, by words, either spoken or written, or by visible representations insults or attempts to insult the religion or the religious beliefs of that class, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to [ten]1 years, or with fine or with both.

The offence under section 295-A PPC comprises the following essential elements: (i) the accused must insult or attempt to insult the religion or religious beliefs of any class of citizens of Pakistan; (ii) such insult must be by words, either spoken or written, or by visible representations; and (iii) the act must be committed with 1 Subs. by Criminal Law (Third Amendment) Ordinance XXI of 1991 (PLD 1991 Cent. 437) w.e.f. 7.7.1991. deliberate and malicious intention to outrage the religious feelings of that class. Commenting on the cognate provision in the Indian Penal Code, Ratanlal & Dhirajlal observe:2 “The essence of the offence under [section 295-A of the Indian Penal Code] is that the insult to religion or the outrage to religious feelings must be the sole, or primary, or at least the deliberate and conscious intention. In order to bring the case within this section, it is not so much the matter of disclosure as the manner of it. The words used should be such as are bound to be regarded by any reasonable man as grossly offensive, provocative, and maliciously and deliberately intended to outrage the feelings of any class of citizens of India. It is no defence to a charge under this section for anyone to plead that he was writing a book in reply to the one written by one professing another religion who has attacked his own religion. The idea of making a separate offence under section 295-A is to punish those who attempt to insult the religion or religious belief of any class of citizens in India. It does not probably relate to any act done with the intention of outraging the religious feelings of any individual or individuals … In order to establish malice as contemplated by section 295-A, it is not necessary to prove that the accused bore ill will or enmity against specific persons. If the injurious act was done voluntarily without a lawful excuse, malice may be presumed. Malice is often not capable of direct and tangible proof and in almost all cases, has to be inferred from the surrounding circumstances, having regard to the setting, background, and connected facts in relation to the offending article. The truth of the allegation is not a good defence to a charge under this section. This section is well within the protection of cl. (2) of Article 19 of the [Indian] Constitution and its validity is beyond question, nor is it inconsistent with the right guaranteed by Article 25(1) of the [Indian] Constitution.”3

In the matter of the Book “Jesus in Heaven on Earth” and in the matter of the petition of The Working Muslim Mission and Literary Trust, Lahore, and of the Civil and Military Gazette Limited, Lahore v. The Crown (PLD 1954 Lahore 724), a Full Bench of this Court held that freedom of speech is not absolute and must cease where discourse degenerates into malice. The Court observed that the sincere and honest propagation of a creed believed to lead to humanity’s salvation is commendable, and incidental harm may be overlooked; however, even such efforts have limits. The dividing line is crossed when speech or writing ceases to advance the legitimate purpose of debate and instead introduces unnecessary, avoidable bitterness or abuse. Approvingly citing Starkie’s Law of Libel and Slander (1897), the Court emphasized that the law punishes not honest error but malicious intent, namely, a wilful intention to insult, 2 Ratanlal & Dhirajlal, The Indian Penal Code, 33rd Edition, p. 1475. 3 Internal citations omitted. pervert, or mislead through abusive language, misrepresentation, or sophistry calculated to mislead the ignorant and unwary. Such malicious or mischievous intention, or an equivalent indifference to societal interests, marks the boundary between lawful expression and culpable wrongdoing.

In The Punjab Religious Book Society, Lahore v. The State (PLD 1960 (W.P.) Lahore 629), a Full Bench of this Court further clarified that section 295-A PPC is attracted “only if it is established that the intention to insult the religious beliefs was deliberate and malicious.” Where the matter objected to, on the ground that it outrages religious feelings, is extremely offensive and lacks any reliable source to justify its acceptance as correct, the court may presume that it was published with the deliberate and malicious intention of insulting the religious beliefs of the followers of the religion concerned or its founder. The same presumption will be raised when the thing objected to indicates that the argument in favour of one religion has sunk to the level of abuse of another. However, in determining such intent, the court must adopt the perspective of a neutral and fair-minded person, “that is to say, a person who is neither connected with the religion of the person who is alleged to have outraged the religious feelings of someone nor with that of the person or persons whose religious feelings are stated to have been outraged.” Furthermore, it should assess the matter from the standpoint of a person who is not hypersensitive but is of normal susceptibilities. Although these observations were made in the context of an impugned publication, they are cited here only insofar as they underline that the matter is to be assessed objectively.

In Muhammad Khalil v. The State (PLD 1962 Lahore 850), this Court held that for section 295-A PPC to apply, it must be proved that the intention to outrage the religious feelings of a class of persons was both deliberate and malicious. Although intention ordinarily implies deliberation, the term “deliberate” was used to denote a conscious and purposeful design, and the additional requirement of malice further elevates the threshold. Accordingly, before holding that section 295-A PPC is attracted, the court must be satisfied that the primary and dominant purpose of the impugned matter was to outrage religious feelings and to do so maliciously.

The present case must be examined in light of the above principles. The allegation against the Petitioner is that he proclaimed himself to be the promised Hazrat Isa (A.S.) who would return by the command of Allah Almighty. On the present record, there is nothing to suggest that he had made any such claim on an earlier occasion by spoken or written words or by visible representations. Therefore, the alleged utterance must be assessed in its surrounding context to ascertain whether it prima facie discloses the intention contemplated by section 295-A PPC.

The Petitioner was under suspension when he visited the office on 19.06.2025. It appears that he had a heated altercation there during which he also abused his superiors and threatened to kill them, and was then removed from the Secretariat by the security staff. It is not alleged that the impugned statement was accompanied by any abusive, derogatory, or insulting language directed at the beliefs of Muslims or Christians. Assessed objectively in accordance with the criteria prescribed by this Court in The Punjab Religious Book Society (PLD 1960 (W.P.) Lahore 629), the requisite mens rea is prima facie absent.

The Petitioner has placed on record certain prescriptions indicating that he has been under medical treatment for psychiatric issues. As noted earlier, these prescriptions cannot, by themselves, establish the defence under section 84 PPC, which remains a question to be determined by the trial court in accordance with law. They nevertheless constitute a circumstance which may be noticed while deciding the bail application for the limited purpose of assessing whether the impugned utterance was the result of a deliberate and malicious design. The prosecution’s reliance on video footage, at this stage, is not determinative.

In view of the above, the case calls for further inquiry within the meaning of section 497(2) Cr.P.C. The investigation has been completed, and the evidence relied upon by the prosecution has been secured. Consequently, the Petitioner’s continued detention appears unnecessary. Accordingly, this bail application is accepted, and the Petitioner is admitted to post-arrest bail subject to furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs. 200,000/- with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial court.

The observations made herein are tentative in nature, made solely for the purpose of deciding the present bail application, and shall not prejudice the case of either party at trial. (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge Ahsan Approved for reporting Judge
